The Hound of the Baskervilles was written by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle and first published in 1902. It is the most famous adventure of the great detective Sherlock Holmes, who solves mysteries not by luck or magic but by careful observation and reason. This retelling keeps the suspense of the moor while making the tale suitable for young readers.

The great detective Sherlock Holmes and his friend Doctor Watson were visited one morning by a country doctor named Mortimer. He carried an old paper telling a chilling legend. Long ago, a cruel lord of the Baskerville family had done a wicked deed upon the moor, and that same night a huge, monstrous hound had hunted him down.

image.note: Sherlock Holmes and Watson listening in a study as Dr Mortimer reads from an old manuscript; a legend unfolding

pages.text: Ever since, the legend said, a phantom hound haunted the moor, and the Baskerville family was cursed. Holmes, a man of pure reason, did not believe in phantoms. But Dr Mortimer had a real and pressing worry. The old master, Sir Charles Baskerville, had just been found dead on the moor, his face frozen in terror.

image.note: A grand moorland manor at dusk; an old man's footprints leading into the mist; foreboding

pages.text: Dr Mortimer told them the strangest detail of all. Near the body, in the soft ground, he had found footprints. Not the footprints of the dead man, but, as he whispered, the footprints of a gigantic hound. Sir Charles had seemingly run in fear until his heart gave out. Was it truly the curse? Or was it murder, made to look like a legend?

image.note: Dr Mortimer pointing gravely at enormous paw prints in the mud near where a body lay; a chilling clue

pages.text: The last living heir, young Sir Henry Baskerville, had just arrived from Canada to claim the family hall. If a killer was at work, Sir Henry was surely in terrible danger. Holmes agreed to take the case at once. But he was too busy in London to travel himself, so he sent his most trusted friend to guard Sir Henry: Doctor Watson.

image.note: A cheerful, sturdy young man, Sir Henry, meeting Holmes and Watson; the detective giving Watson careful instructions

pages.text: Even in London, strange things began. A mysterious bearded man was seen following Sir Henry's cab. A warning note, its words cut from a newspaper, was delivered to his hotel, telling him to keep away from the moor. Someone wanted to frighten Sir Henry off, or worse. Holmes was now certain: this was no ghost story, but the work of a clever and dangerous human mind.

image.note: A hotel room; Sir Henry holding a threatening note made of cut-out newspaper letters; Holmes examining it

pages.text: Brave Sir Henry refused to be scared away from his own home. So Watson travelled with him to the lonely, misty moor and the grim old house of Baskerville Hall, with strict orders to watch everyone, trust no one, and send Holmes a full report of all he saw. The great detective, it seemed, was staying behind in London.

image.note: A carriage crossing a bleak, foggy moor toward a dark stone hall; Watson and Sir Henry aboard; lonely, tense

pages.text: Baskerville Hall was a gloomy place of dark stone, ringed by the wild and empty moor. Watson met the household, including the grave butler Barrymore and his wife. On the very first night, Watson was woken by the sound of a woman weeping, and glimpsed the butler creeping about the dark halls with a candle, holding it to a window as if signalling to someone out on the moor.

image.note: Watson watching the butler hold a candle to a dark window at night, signalling into the fog; suspicious

pages.text: The moor itself held dangers. There was a great bog called the mire, where a wrong step meant a slow and terrible sinking. And a dangerous convict had escaped from a nearby prison and was hiding somewhere out on that very moor. Watson had a great many suspects and secrets to untangle, and the eerie howls that drifted across the moor at night did nothing to calm his nerves.

image.note: A treacherous bog on the moor; a distant escaped prisoner among rocks; wild ponies; danger on all sides

pages.text: Watson met the neighbours. There was a friendly naturalist named Stapleton, who chased butterflies across the moor and knew its safe paths through the deadly mire, and his beautiful sister. There was old Mr Frankland, forever peering through a telescope. Watson watched them all closely, writing careful reports to Holmes, though he could not yet see how the pieces fit together.

image.note: A cheerful man with a butterfly net on the moor beside his sister; Watson observing them thoughtfully

pages.text: Watson solved one mystery, at least. The butler had been signalling to the escaped convict, who turned out to be his wife's own brother. Out of family love, they were secretly leaving him food. It was a sad, human secret, not a wicked one. But it was not the answer to the great mystery, and the true danger to Sir Henry was still out there, unseen.

image.note: The weeping butler's wife confessing; a hidden meal left on the moor for her hunted brother; sympathetic

pages.text: Watson had noticed something troubling. A second man was living secretly out on the moor, hidden among the ancient stone huts, and Watson was determined to find him. One evening he tracked the stranger to his hiding place, crept up, and confronted him at last. Then the figure turned, and Watson's astonishment knew no bounds.

image.note: Watson creeping up on a shadowy figure among ancient stone ruins on the moor at dusk; a confrontation

pages.text: It was Sherlock Holmes. He had never truly stayed in London at all. Secretly, he had come to the moor and lived rough among the stones, so that he could watch everyone unseen, undisturbed by the killer's knowledge. And in his quiet watching, Holmes had already worked out the whole truth. He knew now exactly who was behind the deadly plot.

image.note: The stranger revealed as Holmes himself, calm and clever, in the ruined hut; Watson amazed; a brilliant twist

pages.text: Holmes revealed the culprit. The friendly butterfly-hunter, Stapleton, was secretly a hidden member of the Baskerville family, who meant to murder the other heirs and inherit the fortune himself. He had bought an enormous, savage dog, and painted it with glowing paint to look like the phantom hound of the legend, using the old curse to hide his very real crimes.

image.note: Stapleton revealed as the villain, secretly preparing a huge dog painted to glow; cunning, wicked

pages.text: To catch him, Holmes set a trap using Sir Henry as bait. That night, Sir Henry walked home alone across the moor as arranged, while Holmes, Watson and the police lay hidden in the fog nearby, weapons ready. It was a terrible risk, but the only way to catch the killer in the act. They waited, hearts pounding, as the fog rolled thickly in.

image.note: Sir Henry walking bravely alone across the foggy moor; Holmes, Watson and police hidden in wait; agonising tension

pages.text: Out of the fog it came: an enormous hound, its mouth and eyes glowing with an unearthly fire, bounding straight at Sir Henry. Even knowing the trick, the men were frozen with horror for an instant. Then Holmes and Watson fired, and the great beast fell. It was no phantom at all, only a huge and cruelly treated dog, painted to terrify. The legend was broken.

image.note: The great glowing hound leaping through fog, then falling as shots ring out; terror giving way to relief; not gory

pages.text: The villain Stapleton fled into the darkness, but the moor gave him the justice it had long promised. In his panic he ran into the deadly mire, where one wrong step meant certain doom, and the bog swallowed him whole. Sir Henry was safe, the curse was ended, and the truth stood clear: there had never been a ghost, only a wicked man and a frightened dog.

image.note: The treacherous bog under moonlight, the villain vanished into it; the moor claiming its own; grim justice

pages.text: Back in London, Holmes explained it all to Watson by the fire. Every clue, the warning note, the following stranger, the glowing hound, the safe paths through the mire, had pointed to Stapleton for those who could read them. There are no true phantoms, Holmes reminded his friend. There is only the truth, patiently uncovered, one clear fact at a time.

image.note: Holmes and Watson by a warm London fire, the case solved; the detective explaining calmly; cosy, resolved, closing
